newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar dip takes MCI 90 b.p. under RBNZ optimum.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar dip takes MCI 90 b.p. under RBNZ optimum.

text.p: New Zealand money market monetary conditions eased sharply on Friday with the Monetary Conditions Index (MCI) diverging outside the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's stated comfort zone as the dollar weakened.

By 2358 GMT the MCI NZ/MCI dipped below 735, more than 90 basis points below the RBNZ's optimum level of 825 and well beyond the 775 lower limit of a 50 basis point tolerance band the RBNZ has said the market should bear in mind.
The kiwi dollar traded down to a midday low of about 0.6445/52, about half a U.S. cent below its 0.6497/04 open.
Ninety-day bank bill rates, which together with the dollar's Trade-Weighted Index (TWI) contribute to the MCI index formula, rose to compensate in part for the dollar's slide.
By 0015 GMT the rate had risen to 8.40 percent from an earlier 8.22 percent, but would have to rise much further to take the MCI back towards the Reserve Bank's preferred levels.

Dealers said a comment earlier in the day by Finance Minister Bill Birch, that he was concerned at the possibility of a speculative bubble after recent easing in interest rates and the currency, seemed to have provoked renewed offshore selling.
"It's pretty weak out there. Birch's comment sort of started it, (coming) when the market was looking a little bit soft but as if it was going to have a quiet day.
"After his comments the sentiment was to take the kiwi lower and that seemed to come from offshore," a senior dealer said.
"We were scratching our heads a bit (over the speech)," he added. The dealer said volume was fairly steady and local buying interest was apparent on the dips.
Another dealer said the mid-64 cent area was fairly significant and could be expected to elicit fairly sound exporter buying support for the kiwi.

Several banks are currently predicting the upcoming Household Labour Force Survey (HLFS) due on Tuesday will add further data to a picture of sluggish economic growth, and therefore underpin expectations of a further monetary easing in due course, which would mean the bank tolerating a lower MCI.
However, the senior forex dealer said he felt it was still premature to be expecting an overt easing from the RBNZ.
